article.overview: A closed-loop life-support experiment tests whether biological and physico-chemical processes can recycle the air, water, food and waste of a sealed habitat, so that less material has to be launched from Earth. On the Moon, such an experiment would normally combine higher plants, microorganisms and waste-processing units, and would measure how completely the system closes its loops over time. The sources consulted show no verified lunar flight of a fully closed, crew-operated loop. The closest flown example, Chang'e-4's Lunar Micro Ecosystem, was a sealed biological container rather than a measured recycling system [4][5]. Most quantitative closed-loop evidence comes from ground facilities such as Lunar Palace 1 [1][2] and from ESA's MELiSSA programme [7][8].
article.description: A closed-loop life-support experiment is a sealed or semi-sealed system in which the outputs of one compartment become inputs to another. In a bioregenerative design, photosynthetic organisms take up carbon dioxide, release oxygen and build edible biomass. Microorganisms or chemical units convert urine, inedible plant matter and other waste into nutrients, water and gases that the plants can use [7][8]. The experiment measures inflows, outflows and stored quantities, so that the degree of closure can be expressed as a number rather than a description. Physico-chemical loops, which recycle air and water without living organisms, are an alternative or complement to biological components [7].
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: The purpose is to demonstrate and quantify closure: how much of the oxygen, water, food and nutrients a crew needs can be regenerated in place, how stable the loop remains over time, and which compartment limits performance. The main application is a lunar surface habitat, where resupply from Earth is expensive. An ESA review states that gas and water recycling by physico-chemical processes could be envisioned for any future mission, but that bio-regeneration will be mandatory for a Mars base [7]. A secondary application is biology: the response of organisms to lunar radiation, temperature cycles and reduced gravity. The Chang'e-4 biology payload was an early attempt at this on the lunar surface [4][5].
article.operating_principle: A closed loop works by mass balance. Carbon dioxide from the crew and from microbial respiration is taken up by photosynthetic organisms, which release oxygen and build biomass [6][7]. Nitrogen in urine is converted by nitrifying microorganisms into forms that plants can absorb; the MELiSSA pilot plant includes a nitrifying compartment for this purpose [8]. Solid waste is degraded by microorganisms, releasing mineral nutrients back to the plants [1][2]. Water is recovered by filtration or condensation and returned to the plants and crew [1][3]. Lunar Palace 1 combined higher-plant cultivation, animal protein production, urine nitrogen recycling and solid-waste bioconversion in one facility [1][2]. Measured performance depends on how these processes work together, which is why integration tests matter as much as tests of individual units.
article.scientific_importance: Bioregenerative life support is one of the few approaches that could, in principle, reduce the mass of consumables a long-duration crewed mission must carry, because the same material is reused rather than resupplied [7]. Ground demonstrations are essential because a single flight experiment can test only a small part of a loop. Lunar Palace 1 reported that oxygen and water were recycled and that about 55% of food was regenerated during a 105-day test [1][2]. These figures come from a small number of research groups and were not independently replicated in the sources consulted [1][3]. The field is therefore important mainly as a source of measured closure data, not as evidence that a self-sufficient lunar habitat already exists.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a closed-loop life-support experiment. The examples below are not directly comparable: a 500-cubic-metre ground facility, a lander-borne biological container, a ground pilot plant, a photobioreactor flown on the ISS and a prototype greenhouse answer different questions. Values are given only where a source states them; otherwise they are recorded as not publicly specified.

examples.name: Lunar Palace 1 (ground facility, not flown)
examples.modules: One integrated living module (living, work, bathroom and waste-processing spaces) and two plant cultivation modules.
examples.external_dimensions: not publicly specified in sources consulted
examples.test_summary: 105-day test reported with three crew members [1][3]. One news article refers to two astronauts, which conflicts with the three-person figure [2]. Dates given as February to May 2014 in one institutional record [1] and as a March 2013 start in a news report [3].
examples.reported_results: Oxygen and water recycling; about 55% food regeneration; 20.5% nitrogen recovery from urine; 41% solid-waste degradation [1]. Taken from authors' publications as summarised in secondary sources; full paper not read in this review.

examples.name: Chang'e-4 Lunar Micro Ecosystem (LME)
examples.type: Flown biological container on the lunar farside lander
examples.external_dimensions: not publicly specified in sources consulted
examples.intended_roles: Producers, consumers and decomposers: plants feed fruit flies; yeast breaks down waste [5].
examples.reported_results: Cotton is the only organism with a clear reported result; a later analysis found two cotton leaves where one had been reported [5]. Early reports of rapeseed and potato sprouting conflict with later coverage that none of the other organisms appeared to respond [4][5].
examples.temperature_note: Reported unheated container temperatures fell to about minus 190 C after the first lunar day [4]; from news coverage, not checked against mission data.
examples.publication_status: Team leader stated in 2019 that no scientific papers would be published; no peer-reviewed report found in this review [5].

examples.name: MELiSSA pilot plant (ESA ground demonstrator, not flown as a loop)
examples.facility_location: External ESA laboratory at the Universitat Autonoma de Barcelona
examples.dimensions: not publicly specified in sources consulted
examples.compartment_labels: C1 to C5 used in the literature for principal compartments; sources do not agree on the count [7][8].
examples.integration_status: A 2021 paper describes integration work on compartments 3 (nitrifying packed-bed bioreactor), 4a and 5, with laboratory rats used as a crew mock-up that mimics human respiration [8]. Status may have changed since 2021.

examples.name: ArtemISS (flown photobioreactor on the ISS, MELiSSA-related)
examples.type: Flown photobioreactor experiment on the International Space Station
examples.dimensions: not publicly specified in sources consulted
examples.purpose: Study of how microgravity and space radiation affect growth of Arthrospira [9].
examples.duration: Coverage describes a stay of about one month on the ISS before return to ground laboratories [9].
examples.launch_date_conflict: Reported as September in one source and 9 December in another [9]; unresolved in this review.

examples.name: Inflatable Prototype Lunar/Mars Greenhouse (NASA, prototype tested on Earth)
examples.type: Ground prototype of an inflatable, deployable greenhouse
examples.shape_and_size: Cylindrical, 18 feet (about 5.5 m) long and more than 8 feet (about 2.4 m) in diameter [6].
examples.status: Prototype stage, tested on Earth; next step described as additional lunar greenhouse units for specialised testing; no flight described [6].
examples.function: Crops take up exhaled carbon dioxide and release oxygen; water circulates through the root zone [6].
examples.radiation_protection: Units would likely be buried under soil or regolith, requiring specialised lighting [6].
examples.source_dates: Article dated 24 April 2017; last updated 26 July 2023 [6].

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: The examples differ by an order of magnitude in scale and purpose: a 500-cubic-metre ground facility, a lander-borne biological container with no published dimensions, a ground pilot plant, a flown photobioreactor and a cylindrical prototype greenhouse of about 5.5 m by 2.4 m. No source reviewed gives dimensions for a complete flight-ready closed-loop system, so proportions cannot be generalised.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: No mass is publicly specified for the closed-loop examples in the sources consulted, except that the NASA prototype greenhouse does not state a mass [6]. Launch-mass requirements for a future closed-loop payload cannot be estimated from these sources.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: Power budgets are not publicly specified for any example in the sources consulted. Lighting is an important power demand for plant-based designs [6].

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: A lunar closed-loop experiment must keep living organisms viable in an environment with no atmosphere, large temperature swings, high radiation and fine dust. Plants and microorganisms need controlled light, temperature, humidity and gas composition, which in turn require power and thermal management. Radiation protection is a design driver: the NASA prototype concept would sit under regolith, which in turn requires specialised lighting [6]. The organisms must also tolerate the reduced-gravity conditions of the mission; the ArtemISS flight was designed in part to study how microgravity affects Arthrospira growth [9]. Sealing and contamination control matter because a disturbed microbial population can change the performance of a whole loop. These are engineering considerations rather than values taken from a specific source.
article.limitations: A closed loop is only as strong as its weakest compartment, and biological performance can drift with light, temperature, nutrient balance and microbial populations. Ground facilities such as Lunar Palace 1 operate under controlled conditions that cannot reproduce all lunar surface effects. Flown biological experiments have been small and short compared with a crewed habitat [4][9]. No source reviewed describes a lunar closed loop operating with a crew for a full mission. Biological output is also difficult to standardise across species, so results from one organism cannot be transferred to a complete system.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: A closed-loop experiment would be delivered as a payload module or as a package on a lander, with plants, microorganisms, water, lighting and sealed containers each needing separate handling and launch-safety review. No lander or spacecraft compatibility has been verified.
transportation_process: Earth integration: integrate the biological payload and its sealed containers, lighting, water and power interfaces into a lander payload; the Chang'e-4 LME was delivered as a payload on a lander [4].
Launch and lunar transfer: no mass or volume for a closed-loop system is given in the sources reviewed, so launch-mass requirements cannot be estimated.

Landing and deployment: the NASA prototype concept would be buried under regolith for radiation protection, implying excavation or a mechanical deployment capability [6]; the deployment mechanism for the LME is not described in the sources.
Power and data: lighting is an important power demand for plant-based designs [6]; no power budgets are given in the sources reviewed.
Thermal and mechanical interfaces: the reported temperature excursion of the Chang'e-4 container, to about minus 190 C, shows that thermal insulation or heating is a critical interface [4].
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Not publicly specified for a closed-loop payload. The NASA prototype concept implies burial under regolith [6]. The Chang'e-4 LME deployment mechanism is not described in the sources reviewed.
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: Chang'e-4 Lunar Micro Ecosystem delivered on a lunar farside lander in early 2019 [4][5]. Lunar Palace 1 is a ground facility and was never transported [1][2].
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No specific lander, rover or spacecraft compatibility has been verified. A closed-loop payload should not be assigned to a named lander until its mass, dimensions, power, thermal and interface data are compared with verified spacecraft specifications.

article.historical_significance: ESA's MELiSSA programme, begun in 1989, is a long-running European effort to develop a closed bioregenerative life-support system for lunar bases and long-term missions [7]. The Chang'e-4 LME is a widely reported biological experiment on the lunar farside, although its scientific results have not been published in peer-reviewed form as far as this review could establish [4][5]. Lunar Palace 1's 105-day test in 2014 is a widely reported ground closed-loop test in a lunar-style facility [1][2][3]. A later 370-day integrated test in an upgraded facility, reported as Lunar Palace 365, has been cited in secondary summaries but was not verified against a primary source in this review. A TU Delft study reported no difference between terrestrial and ISS samples for several MELiSSA-relevant microbial strains after a 7-day ISS exposure, which supports flight-testing of loop components [11]. A 2026 viewpoint reported by Imperial College London argues that plants should be treated as core life-support infrastructure and proposes a readiness scale for bioregenerative systems [12].
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: No single design defines a closed-loop life-support experiment, so results from ground facilities, flown photobioreactors and single-organism lunar tests cannot be combined into one specification. The quantitative results cited for Lunar Palace 1 come mainly from authors affiliated with the facility and from secondary summaries, not from full texts checked in this review [1][2][3]. Reported dates for the 2014 test differ between sources [1][3]. The Chang'e-4 biological results are contested between early news reports and later coverage, and no peer-reviewed paper was found [4][5]. The ArtemISS launch date is reported inconsistently [9]. Engineering values for the NASA prototype greenhouse, including mass and power, are not publicly specified [6]. Mass, power and dimensions for most examples are not publicly specified in the sources consulted. This article does not describe any closed-loop system as flight-proven; the sources reviewed describe only component-level experiments in space, such as plant cultivation, photobioreactor and microbial tests, and no full loop has been demonstrated there [10].

image_handling.url_policy: All URL query strings and fragments removed. No images were included because no direct image asset could be verified in this run; the Leonard David and Universe Today pages were not used as image sources.

data_quality_notes: No images included: no direct, official image asset URL was verified in this run, so none were invented or taken from search-result thumbnails.

Lunar Palace 1 figures (55% food regeneration, 20.5% nitrogen recovery, 41% solid-waste degradation, 500 m3 volume, 160 m2 floor area, 36 m2 plant area) come from search-result summaries and secondary pages; the Fu et al. 2016 full text was not read.
Lunar Palace 1 crew count conflicts across sources (three volunteers versus two astronauts) and the start date conflicts (February 2014 versus March 2013).
Chang'e-4 LME organism results conflict between early reports (rapeseed and potato sprouting) and later coverage (no response from other organisms); no peer-reviewed paper located.
The minus 190 C container temperature for Chang'e-4 comes from news coverage and is not checked against mission telemetry.
ArtemISS launch date conflicts between ESA and SCK CEN coverage (September versus 9 December); unresolved.

MELiSSA compartment count differs between sources; the ESA life-support page returned 404 and the MELiSSA pilot-plant claims rely on search excerpts and a 2021 paper whose PDF was not readable in this run.
The npj Microgravity 2023 review and Imperial College 2026 viewpoint were not read in full; statements are from search summaries.

No mass, dimensions or power values are published in the sources consulted for any closed-loop example except the Lunar Palace 1 volume and floor area and the NASA prototype size; all other numeric fields are null.

Mid-range claims about the lunar relevance of MELiSSA and of plant-based greenhouses are based on programme and agency statements, not on verified lunar mission plans. No funded lunar flight of a closed loop was found.
